title: 5 Survival Lessons When The Pressure Never Stops
author: Chiarelli, Andrea
summary: Andrea Chiarelli and therapist Nicole Ohebshalom identify survival lessons for founders, executives, and consultants operating under unrelenting pressure—where the inbox never sleeps, capital cycles never end, and the load is structurally infinite. The core reframe is that standard productivity advice fails in these environments because it assumes a clearing point that never arrives. The real skill is learning to operate well at altitude indefinitely: guarding a few critical hours, accepting difficulty as permanent, and stopping before exhaustion degrades judgement.
points: Standard productivity tools—time-blocking, priority matrices, the two-minute rule—assume a finite work queue and fail in high-pressure environments because the load never clears.
The question 'how do I get on top of everything?' is the wrong question; high-performing leaders learn to ask 'how do I operate well at altitude for years?' instead.
Guarding your best hours means declining things that look perfectly reasonable on a calendar—the hard part isn't recognising that bandwidth is finite but following through on that recognition.
Leaders who push through exhausted Fridays pay the cost the following week in poor decisions and slow thinking; the recovery debt consistently exceeds the apparent productivity gain.
In high-pressure environments, constant difficulty is not a sign that something is wrong—it is the permanent, ordinary texture of the job itself.
quotes: The instinctive question, the one all the productivity tools are built to answer, is “how do I get on top of everything?” The question these leaders have learned to ask instead is “how do I keep functioning well inside something I will never be on top of?” This question is uncomfortable, because answering it means giving up the fantasy that if you just found the right system or worked the right number of hours, the load would finally resolve and you could relax.

Once you stop waiting for the queue to clear and accept that the job is to operate well at altitude for years, the questions turn concrete: which hours you guard, what you allow to drop, how you build recovery in, who you tell the truth to, and how you keep the role from swallowing the self.

The pressure in Silicon Valley, where Nicole Ohebshalom, PhD is a therapist to CEOs, founders, engineers and their families, has some defining features: Teams are distributed across time zones, so the inbox never sleeps; by the time you’ve cleared London, San Francisco is waking up.

The hard part isn’t recognising that bandwidth is finite, but following through on this concept: guarding your best hours means declining things that look perfectly reasonable on the calendar and doing it consistently enough that people stop expecting otherwise.

Every one of these techniques treats the load as finite and the main problem as sequencing: you have a fixed pile of work, and the skill is putting it in the right order so that the important things get done and the rest waits for its turn.

They arrived at the rule through experimentation, by noticing that pushing through those Fridays reliably cost them more the following week in poor calls and slow thinking, as well as small things they would normally have caught.
